query: What are emotional wounds, and how do they actually heal?
why_in_two_sentences: Corner Canyon gives an LCSW-bylined types-symptoms-healing overview (a Bourbeau-style five-wound list, named therapies, and a concrete grounding toolkit) and Psychology Today offers a function-based wound-versus-trauma spectrum from a trauma author, but both stay at the level of labels and general self-care without explaining the machinery that keeps a wound running. Ours out-covers them on structure (need/belief/behavior), the re-enactment-versus-memory distinction, why insight fails, and the resolved-day-to-day picture, trailing only on named evidence-based therapies and a same-day distress toolkit.
what_the_winner_does_that_we_dont: Names specific evidence-based therapies and what each targets: CBT for reframing negative thought patterns and EMDR for trauma (Corner Canyon)
Gives a concrete same-day distress toolkit for when emotion is overwhelming: 5-4-3-2-1 sensory grounding, holding an ice cube, warm shower, unsent letters, uncensored journaling (Corner Canyon)
Provides an explicit symptom checklist grouped as mental (sadness, anger/irritability, fear/anxiety) and behavioral (social withdrawal, aggression/passive-aggression) so a reader can self-screen
Fronts a credentialed clinician byline (LCSW, 30 years) and a trauma-author byline, establishing authority our page's founder byline does not match
what_we_do_that_they_dont: Breaks a wound into three separable parts (unmet need, first-person belief, protective behavior) and states that the need is the layer that must change, giving a why-it-heals mechanism neither competitor supplies
Draws the re-enactment-versus-memory line: a bad memory sits still and gets recalled, a wound arrives as a reflex without consulting memory, which is the page's core diagnostic
Explains why contradictory behaviors (seeking closeness vs pushing it away) protect the same need, and why swapping one for the other changes nothing
Separates 'name the wound' (describes history) from 'name the need' (a sentence you can say to another person) and gives a work-backward-from-three-moments exercise
Shows the resolved end concretely on an ordinary week (a request without a pre-apology, a no without three sentences of justification) and answers why therapy/self-help books alone did not fix it

above_the_fold.ours: H1 is the exact query; a short-answer box defines a wound as protection that outlived its conditions and states wounds resolve when the need gets met in the present, then an identify-box of five verbatim beliefs. Strong recognition plus a definition-and-healing promise that earns the scroll.
above_the_fold.theirs: Corner Canyon opens with a long author bio and table of contents before the content, pushing the actual definition below the fold; the fold sells the clinic's authority more than it hooks the reader's problem.

questions_they_answer_that_we_dont: What are the symptoms of unresolved emotional wounds?
What therapies help heal emotional wounds (CBT, EMDR)?
What can I do right now when the emotional pain feels overwhelming?
trust_signals: Both competitors carry named credentialed authors (an LCSW with 30 years, a published trauma clinician) and name specific therapy modalities, while ours leads on lived specificity and mechanism but names a founder author with no clinical credential and no cited modalities.
one_change_with_most_traffic_impact: Add a short 'how healing actually happens, including with a professional' block that names CBT and EMDR for the trauma-range wounds and gives one concrete same-day grounding practice (e.g. 5-4-3-2-1), so the 'how do they heal' half of the query is answered with the modality names searchers expect without diluting the need-gets-met mechanism.
